content.text: Physics is the study of the natural world, from the smallest subatomic particles to the largest structures in the universe. To describe and understand the physical world, we need a precise language — one built on
. Every measurement in physics consists of a numerical value and a unit. Saying that a table is "2" long is meaningless; saying it is "2 metres" long gives us clear, useful information.

In this lesson, we will explore the international system of units (SI), learn how to work with derived units and prefixes, distinguish between scalar and vector quantities, and develop skills in unit conversion and dimensional analysis. These foundational tools are essential for every topic you will study in physics.
is any property of a material or system that can be measured or calculated. Examples include length, mass, time, temperature, electric current, speed, force, and energy.
For example, a distance of 5.0 metres has a magnitude of 5.0 and a unit of metres (m).
is the internationally agreed system of units used in science. It is built on seven

| Base Quantity | Symbol | SI Base Unit | Unit Symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Length | $l$ | metre | m |
| Mass | $m$ | kilogram | kg |
| Time | $t$ | second | s |
| Electric current | $I$ | ampere | A |
| Temperature | $T$ | kelvin | K |
| Amount of substance | $n$ | mole | mol |
| Luminous intensity | $I_v$ | candela | cd |
These seven base units are the foundation of the entire SI system. Every other unit in physics can be expressed as a combination of these base units.
Why do we need a standard system?

Imagine if every country used different units for the same quantity. Communication would be extremely difficult, and errors would be common. In fact, in 1999, NASA lost a $125 million Mars orbiter because one engineering team used metric units while another used imperial units. The SI system prevents such disasters by providing a universal standard.
are formed by combining base units through multiplication or division. They are used for quantities that are defined in terms of the base quantities.
Here are some important derived units:

| Quantity | Formula | Derived Unit | Unit Symbol | In Base Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Area | length × width | square metre | m² | m² |
| Volume | length × width × height | cubic metre | m³ | m³ |
| Speed/Velocity | distance ÷ time | metre per second | m/s | m s⁻¹ |
| Acceleration | velocity ÷ time | metre per second squared | m/s² | m s⁻² |
| Force | mass × acceleration | newton | N | kg m s⁻² |
| Energy/Work | force × distance | joule | J | kg m² s⁻² |
| Power | energy ÷ time | watt | W | kg m² s⁻³ |
| Pressure | force ÷ area | pascal | Pa | kg m⁻¹ s⁻² |
| Density | mass ÷ volume | kilogram per cubic metre | kg/m³ | kg m⁻³ |
| Frequency | 1 ÷ time | hertz | Hz | s⁻¹ |
| Charge | current × time | coulomb | C | A s |
| Voltage | energy ÷ charge | volt | V | kg m² s⁻³ A⁻¹ |
| Resistance | voltage ÷ current | ohm | Ω | kg m² s⁻³ A⁻² |

Every physical quantity can be expressed in terms of fundamental dimensions:
For example, speed has dimensions [L][T]⁻¹ (length divided by time), and force has dimensions [M][L][T]⁻² (from
In any valid physics equation, the dimensions on both sides must match.
Consider the equation for kinetic energy:
Left side: Energy has units of joules = kg m² s⁻², so dimensions are [M][L]²[T]⁻².
Right side: mass × velocity² = kg × (m/s)² = kg × m² s⁻² = [M][L]²[T]⁻².
Both sides match, so the equation is dimensionally consistent. Note that dimensional analysis cannot verify dimensionless constants (like the ½), but it can catch errors where units do not balance.

"Mass and weight are the same thing."

Mass (measured in kg) is the amount of matter in an object and does not change with location. Weight (measured in N) is the gravitational force on an object and changes depending on the gravitational field strength. We will explore this further in a later lesson.
A value of 5000 mm is not larger than 6 m. You must convert to the same unit before comparing: 5000 mm = 5 m, which is less than 6 m.
Zeros between non-zero digits (e.g., 305) and trailing zeros after a decimal point (e.g., 2.50) are significant. Only leading zeros (e.g., 0.003) are not significant.

Speed is a scalar (magnitude only), while velocity is a vector (magnitude and direction). An object moving at constant speed in a circle has changing velocity because its direction is constantly changing.
"You can add scalar and vector quantities."
Scalars and vectors follow different addition rules. You cannot directly add 5 m (distance) and 5 m north (displacement) in a meaningful way.
